paper_metadata.title: Constructing Knowledge Graphs from Text Using Large Language Models: Scoping Review
paper_metadata.venue: Companion Proceedings of the 40th Brazilian Symposium on Data Bases
paper_metadata.abstract: The use of Large Language Models (LLMs) for Knowledge Graph (KG) construction has gained significant traction, yet the field lacks methodological standardization. This study conducts a scope review following the PRISMA framework to map existing techniques and categorize them into four main approaches: (i) RDF-Based; (ii) Prompt-Based; (iii) RAG-Based; and (iv) Hybrid Pipelines. Analyzing 126 primary studies, the authors identify scalability and automation as benefits, alongside low precision and manual curation as challenges.

problem_addressed: The paper addresses the lack of methodological standardization and consolidated evidence about techniques that use LLMs to construct knowledge graphs from unstructured text. Its objective is to map existing approaches, compare their effectiveness and characteristics, and identify benefits, limitations, and research gaps.

methodology.description: This is a PRISMA-based scoping review, not a single Text-to-KG system. The review has planning, execution, and reporting phases. It searches Scopus, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, and ACM using the query “Knowledge Graph” AND (“Large Language Model” OR “LLM” OR “Generative Pre-trained Transformers”) AND text; screens studies using eligibility criteria; extracts bibliographic and methodological information; and synthesizes 126 included primary studies into four categories. The reviewed execution patterns are: RDF-based ontology selection, LLM-assisted extraction and RDF serialization; prompt-based direct structured-triple extraction; RAG-based retrieval followed by enriched LLM triple generation and graph integration; and hybrid NLP extraction followed by LLM refinement, validation, or augmentation and graph storage.

ontology_or_schema_use.value: Ontology/schema use varies by reviewed category. RDF-Based methods explicitly define a domain and select existing ontologies, provide ontology text, links, or descriptions to the LLM, align extracted elements with established vocabularies, serialize RDF, and store triples. Prompt-Based methods generally do not rely on predefined ontologies. RAG-Based methods use external document bases, wikis, databases, or existing graphs as retrieved context but usually do not enforce formal schema alignment. Hybrid Pipelines may align final triples with ontologies depending on their NLP configuration.

evaluation.setting: Scoping-review synthesis of primary studies rather than a new controlled experiment. The review applied PRISMA-style identification, screening, eligibility, and inclusion; it reports category counts, model/domain frequencies, and qualitative cross-study comparisons, while noting heterogeneous metrics and evaluation practices.

value: The review analyzed 126 primary studies and grouped them into four categories: RDF-Based (50 studies), Prompt-Based (35), RAG-Based (22), and Hybrid Pipelines (19).
Among 36 studies that compared multiple models, OpenAI GPT was most frequently used, followed by LLAMA and ChatGLM; GPT-4 and its branches were the most common GPT versions.
When application domains were specified, general knowledge was most frequent, followed by health and manufacturing processes.
The review identifies automation, scalability, and precision as recurring advantages, and manual curation, limited generalization, and low precision as recurring limitations.

RDF-Based methods emphasize formal ontologies, RDF serialization, semantic interoperability, and SPARQL querying; Prompt-Based methods emphasize direct triple extraction without supervised fine-tuning or predefined ontologies; RAG-Based methods add retrieved external context; Hybrid Pipelines combine classical NLP extraction with LLM refinement, validation, or augmentation.

The review reports that no single approach resolves all challenges and that prompt- and RAG-based methods are more flexible but less reproducible, while RDF-based and hybrid methods provide greater structural control and interpretability.

value: The review uses an explicit PRISMA-adapted protocol with stated research questions, databases, search string, eligibility criteria, extraction stages, and synthesis procedure.

It provides a compact taxonomy of four recurring LLM-based KG-construction patterns and further subdivides prompt-based methods into zero-shot prompting, sequential prompt chaining, and template-driven prompting.
It compares approaches along useful dimensions: ontology alignment, prompting role, supervision, reproducibility, semantic control, scalability, and interpretability.
It identifies recurring cross-study benefits and limitations rather than presenting only isolated paper summaries.

value: Review-level inference: the four categories do not map cleanly onto the repository's finer-grained Text-to-KG taxonomy and mix architectural choices (RDF, RAG, hybrid) with prompting strategies and supervision settings.
The review reports heterogeneous metrics and no standardized benchmarks, limiting direct comparison across studies.

The category counts are internally inconsistent: the four reported counts sum to 126, but the text elsewhere states that 19 Hybrid Pipeline studies include 13 supervised fine-tuning studies and also presents the total as 126 without a clear overlap policy.

The review's cross-study claims about precision, accuracy, reproducibility, and model prevalence are summarized qualitatively, with limited method-, dataset-, split-, and metric-level quantitative evidence.
